analysis.one_liner: Ends federal subsidies, tax breaks, and royalty discounts for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: Referred to nine House committees in April 2015, the bill never received a single hearing or vote and expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap dozens of federal giveaways to oil, gas, and coal companies: royalty discounts and the 12.5% minimum royalty on federal and offshore leases, more than a dozen special tax breaks, the cap on what companies owe for offshore oil spills, and federal financing of fossil-fuel projects through the Export-Import Bank, the World Bank, and rural electrification loans. It would also raise the per-barrel fee that funds oil-spill cleanups and add a 13% tax on oil and gas taken from the Gulf of Mexico. The bill's own findings put federal fossil-fuel subsidies at $72 billion from 2002 to 2008, against $12.2 billion for renewables.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would keep more of the value of publicly owned coal, oil, and gas through higher royalties and closed tax loopholes. Coastal communities and fishermen, who would no longer face a legal ceiling on what a spilling company must pay. And, relatively, the renewable energy industry, which competes against fossil fuels that enjoy subsidized financing and research support.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum royalty on federal coal, oil, and gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75% and repeals offshore royalty relief, so public resources return more money to taxpayers.

Terminates more than a dozen fossil-fuel tax preferences, including expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery and marginal-well credits, and the corporate tax exemption for fossil-fuel master limited partnerships.

Removes the cap on spill liability for offshore facilities and for pipelines carrying tar-sands-type oil, so the company that causes a spill pays the full cost of the damage instead of a capped amount.

Bars federal money from financing fossil-fuel projects: it rescinds unobligated funds and bans future financing through the World Bank, Export-Import Bank, and OPIC, blocks DOE loan guarantees and rural electrification loans for fossil projects, and stops Transportation Department grants for rail or port projects that transport fossil fuel.

Adds a 13% tax on oil and gas produced from the Gulf of Mexico outer continental shelf (crediting royalties already paid) and raises the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund fee from 8 to 10 cents per barrel.
Terminates the Department of Energy's Office of Fossil Energy Research and Development and directs Treasury to inventory every remaining fossil-fuel subsidy in federal law.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, through higher royalties, repealed tax breaks, a new 13% Gulf severance tax, higher spill fees, and uncapped spill liability. Some of those costs would likely be passed through to consumers in fuel prices, and small independent drillers — not just the large corporations — rely on several of the repealed tax provisions.

drawbacks.text: The higher per-barrel spill-fund fee and the new 13% Gulf severance tax would likely be passed into fuel prices, so part of the cost lands on consumers at the pump.

Several repealed provisions — the marginal-well credit, percentage depletion, and expensing of intangible drilling costs — are used heavily by small independent producers, which the bill would hit harder than the major oil companies.

The bill repeals the 45Q carbon-sequestration credit and terminates DOE's fossil-energy research office, cutting federal support for carbon capture technology that many climate policy analysts consider necessary.

Lifting the cap on offshore spill liability would raise insurance and operating costs for offshore operators and pipeline companies; defenders of caps argue they balance deterrence against keeping operations viable.
Rural electric utilities would lose access to Rural Electrification Act loans for any project using fossil fuel, with no transition exception like the one the bill provides for poor countries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and broad: billions of dollars in subsidies end, public lands and waters return more revenue, and companies that cause spills bear the full cost. The honest costs are real but smaller: modest consumer price pass-through, a sharper blow to small drillers and coal-dependent communities than to the majors, and the loss of carbon-capture incentives at a time when some argue that technology needs federal support. The bill is a blunt sweep rather than a finely tuned reform, but its costs are modest next to what it claws back from highly profitable industries.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to nine committees and five subcommittees, none ever held a hearing or brought it up, and it quietly expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on April 22, 2015.
The same day, it was referred to nine standing committees — Ways and Means plus eight others — a routing under which every panel with jurisdiction must act before a bill can move.
Between April and August 2015 it was passed down to five subcommittees; those subcommittee referrals were the bill's last recorded actions.
No committee ever held a hearing or reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

The bill's findings section put federal fossil-fuel subsidies at $72 billion from 2002 to 2008 versus $12.2 billion for renewables, and tallied $1.8 billion in lobbying by the oil, gas, coal, and utility industries from 2010 to 2014.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel producers came out ahead: they kept the royalty discounts, tax preferences, liability caps, and federal financing that the bill would have ended, and taxpayers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act on April 22, 2015 and was its only sponsor.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Had pledged at G20 summits to phase out fossil-fuel subsidies and proposed repealing many of the same tax breaks in his annual budgets; the bill never reached his desk.

against.name: Republican chairs of the nine committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Let the bill sit without a hearing or markup in any of the nine committees to which it was referred; the last action was a subcommittee referral in August 2015.

against.name: Oil, gas, coal, and utility industries
against.what_they_did: Lobbied through this period to preserve fossil-fuel tax preferences, royalty terms, and federal financing; the bill's own findings cite $1.8 billion in industry lobbying from 2010 to 2014.

sides.party_line_note: The only members ever attached to the bill were Democrats — sponsor Keith Ellison and two Democratic cosponsors; no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever held to test either full caucus.

industries.note: Would lose offshore royalty relief, a minimum royalty raise from 12.5% to 18.75%, roughly a dozen tax preferences, the offshore spill liability cap, a new 13% Gulf severance tax, and a higher spill-fund fee. The bill's findings cited $1.8 billion in industry lobbying from 2010 to 2014 protecting these terms.

Faces the 18.75% minimum royalty on federal leases, repeal of percentage depletion and of capital-gains treatment for coal royalties, loss of LIFO accounting, and a fair-market-value study of underpriced Powder River Basin leases.

Loses access to federal financing: rescinded funds and a ban on future support through the World Bank, Export-Import Bank, OPIC, DOE loan guarantees, and rural electrification loans for fossil projects.

industries.industry: Investors in fossil-fuel master limited partnerships
industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax exemption for publicly traded partnerships earning fossil-fuel income, closing a structure that lets these investors skip a layer of tax.
Barred from receiving Transportation Department grants or loans for projects that transport fossil fuel, a narrow but real loss of public funding for their infrastructure.
With the DOE fossil-energy research office terminated and ARPA-E funds restricted to non-fossil projects, subsidized competition shrinks and the subsidy playing field levels.
